messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prison Guard
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 42

He is twenty-eight years old, a prison guard at a maximum-security facility, married for three years to a woman named Elena. They live in a small apartment on the south side of the city, near the neighborhood where he grew up. He does not talk about his brother Marco. That is the first thing he says in session, his voice flat: “I don’t talk about him.”

The day Marco died, he was in the control room during second shift. He remembers the exact moment—the phone rang, his mother screaming on the other end. “Marco, Marco, they shot him.” He could not leave. There was a code blue in D-block, inmates fighting, and the sergeant needed every body on the floor. He stayed at his post for four more hours, watching monitors, holding the phone in his pocket. By the time he got to the hospital, Marco was already gone. A drive-by, mistaken identity, wrong place wrong time. He was twenty-two.

The funeral was a blur of incense and his aunt’s wailing. He did not cry. He put on his uniform the next morning and went back to work. Elena begged him to take time off. He said he couldn’t, said the unit was short-staffed, said he needed to keep busy. That was six months ago.

Now he works double shifts whenever he can. He volunteers for the dangerous posts—the segregation unit, the intake processing line—places where he has to stay alert. But the alertness has become something else. He notices things that others miss: the way an inmate shifts his weight before a fight, the wrong sound of a gate latch, the faint smell of smoke from a contraband lighter. At night, he lies awake replaying every interaction from the day, scanning for mistakes. He has started checking his car locks three times before he drives home. He avoids the corner where Marco was killed, taking the long way even if it adds forty minutes to his commute.

His wife says he is not the same. He does not argue. He knows he is different. He can feel a wall inside him, thick and cold, that he uses to push through each day. When Elena reaches for him in bed, he pretends to be asleep. When she tries to talk about Marco, he walks out of the room. He cannot stand the weight of her grief on top of his own. He tells himself he is fine. He tells himself he is handling it.

But the dreams come anyway. In them, Marco is still alive, standing in the doorway of the prison break room, asking why he did not answer the phone. He wakes up sweating, heart hammering, convinced someone has broken into the apartment. Some nights he gets up and sits in the dark living room, watching the street through the blinds until dawn.

At work, a young inmate who looks like Marco—same jaw, same nervous laugh—got transferred onto his block last month. He had to request a reassignment. He told his supervisor it was a security concern. The real reason is that every time he sees that kid, he feels a pressure behind his eyes that he cannot explain. He is afraid he might do something, say something.

He is here because Elena made an appointment for him. He sits in the chair with his arms crossed, his gaze fixed on a spot on the wall. He says he does not know what talking will do. He says Marco is dead and there is nothing to change. But his hands are shaking, and he keeps looking at the door. When he talks about the drive-by, his sentences break apart, start and stop. He says he should have been there. He says he should have answered the phone faster. He says maybe if he had left his post, if he had driven faster, he could have been there to hold a towel to the wound, to tell Marco it would be okay. He knows it is not rational. He cannot stop thinking it.
